content: Write a LinkedIn post about hiring for attitude over experience.

**The résumé tells you where someone's been. It doesn't tell you where they're going.**

I've stopped leading with "Have you done this before?"

Not because experience doesn't matter — it does. But I've watched plenty of perfectly qualified people stall out, and plenty of "underqualified" ones become the person everyone wants on their project.

The difference was almost never raw skill. It was how they behaved when they didn't know something.

The ones who worked out tended to:
→ Say "I don't know" quickly, then go find out
→ Treat feedback as information, not an attack
→ Ask questions that showed they'd already wrestled with the problem
→ Care whether the work was actually good, not just finished

You can teach the software. You can teach the process. It's much harder to teach someone to care.

One caveat, because this advice gets abused: "hire for attitude" too often becomes code for "hire people I'd grab a beer with." That's how teams end up looking and thinking exactly alike. Attitude isn't likeability. It's curiosity, ownership, and how someone handles being wrong — and those are things you can actually assess with structured questions.

So now I ask candidates about the last time they were completely out of their depth. What they did. What they'd do differently. Whether they're honest about the part they got wrong.

That answer tells me more than ten years on a CV.

What's the best "unqualified" hire you've ever made?

---

A few notes: if you have a real example of a hire like this, drop a sentence about them after the opening — specifics outperform generalities on LinkedIn every time. Happy to make this shorter, punchier, or more story-driven, or add a couple of hashtags if that fits your usual posting style.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

**"Hire for attitude, train for skill" is where the conversation starts, not where it ends.**

We all nod at it. Then we go back to filtering on years-in-role because attitude is hard to evidence in a hiring committee and "8 years at a competitor" isn't.

The gap isn't belief. It's assessment.

A few things that have actually moved the needle for me:

**Score the behaviour, not the vibe.** If your attitude signal lives in the unstructured chat at the end, you're measuring rapport. Put it in the scorecard with defined anchors, or it will quietly collapse into "people like me."

**Probe the failure, not the success.** Anyone can narrate a win. Ask about a project that went badly and listen for where the agency sits in the story. Someone who can name their own contribution to a mess without performing contrition is rare and worth a lot.

**Price the ramp honestly.** This is the part the LinkedIn version of the advice skips. A high-potential hire with a skills gap is a real cost — to your senior people, to your delivery dates, to the hire themselves if nobody has bandwidth to coach them. Attitude hires fail most often not because we misjudged the person, but because we didn't have the capacity to support the bet we made.

**Watch what it does to your bar.** "Attitude over experience" can become a rationalisation for hiring cheap and hoping. If the same reasoning keeps producing candidates who are junior, underpaid, and conveniently agreeable, that's not a philosophy — that's a budget.

The teams that get this right aren't the ones that believe in potential hardest. They're the ones that built the scaffolding to convert it.

Where does this break down for you — the assessment, or the support after the offer?

---

I've assumed a reader who's run hiring loops and is bored of the premise, so this argues with the cliché rather than making the case for it. If your audience skews more toward founders doing their first few hires, or toward talent acquisition specifically, I can shift the emphasis — the ramp-cost point and the budget point land differently depending on who's paying for the mistake.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

**Everyone believes in hiring for attitude. Almost nobody has built the machinery to do it.**

The gap isn't conviction — it's assessment and capacity.

**Assessment:** if your attitude signal lives in the unstructured chat at the end, you're measuring rapport, not attitude. Put it in the scorecard with defined anchors, or it collapses into "people like me." And probe failure, not success — anyone can narrate a win. Listen for where the agency sits when the story goes badly.

**Capacity:** a high-potential hire with a skills gap is a real cost — to your seniors, your dates, and to the hire themselves if nobody has bandwidth to coach. These bets fail less often because we misjudged the person, and more often because we couldn't support the bet we made.

One flag: if "attitude over experience" keeps producing candidates who are junior, cheap, and conveniently agreeable, that's not a philosophy. That's a budget.

Where does it break for you — the assessment, or the support after the offer?

---

That's about 170 words, down from ~350. I cut the two weaker scaffolding points and folded the failure-probe into the assessment section to keep the two-part structure intact. If the placement is tight on space, the closing question is the easiest thing to drop; if it's a newsletter or something with more room to breathe, I'd put the ramp-cost point back as its own beat.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

I removed the sentence about why these bets fail — "less often because we misjudged the person, more often because we couldn't support the bet" — since that was the one line asserting an observed outcome. Everything else is unchanged.

Worth knowing: that sentence was carrying the argumentative weight of the Capacity section. Without it, that beat now just states that ramp-up costs something, which is closer to a truism. If you want the section to earn its place again, a non-empirical version could do it — something framed as a question or a principle rather than a finding. Say the word and I'll draft one, but I've left it alone for now as you asked.
